passage:
Dalia had noticed it by her third month at the Rotterdam studio: nobody picked a colour anymore. They made three versions and waited for Elif. Elif chose the blue, moved the logo two millimetres, rewrote the email to the printer. At Thursday stand-ups Joost said 'whatever Elif thinks' so often it had become a joke no one laughed at.
The museum poster went out nine days late. Dalia didn't say Elif was controlling. She brought the calendar instead.
'On the last two jobs, most of the delay was work sitting in the approval pile,' she said. 'If we decide type and colour inside the brand guide, and you review the final draft only, I think we'd hit our dates.'
Elif studied the calendar for a long moment. 'Show me one job done that way.'

qa.q: How late did the museum poster go out?
qa.a: Nine days late.

qa.q: What did Dalia think was really slowing the studio down?
qa.a: She thought the delays came from work sitting in the approval pile, because the team had stopped choosing and waited for Elif.

qa.q: Why did Dalia choose to bring the calendar instead of calling Elif controlling?
qa.a: The dates kept the talk on results that Elif could check rather than on Elif's character, and that made a trial possible.

qa.q: How might Elif feel being shown the calendar instead of being called controlling?
qa.a: Elif might feel less attacked and more able to weigh the idea, since the dates are facts to check; 'Show me one job done that way' suggests cautious openness.

grounding: Shows a team watching Elif decide every detail, the resulting delays and passivity, and feedback framed around results rather than personality.

passage:
Every Monday at the district library, Irfan handed out a typed sheet: which books go on the front shelf, which chair the storyteller sits in, even what colour paper for the craft table. Simran, who ran the children's corner with two others, watched her colleagues stop bringing ideas. Kusum used to invent puppet voices; now she read the sheet aloud and went home on time.
Saturday storytime, once packed with thirty kids, had shrunk to about twelve.
Simran waited for the monthly meeting. 'Sir, can I show you the sign-in book? Attendance was highest in the months we tried new formats. Could each of us plan one Saturday a month, and you look at the numbers after?'
Irfan frowned at the register, then turned a page back, and another. 'One Saturday,' he said. 'We'll see.'

qa.q: How many kids came to Saturday storytime before it shrank?
qa.a: It was once packed with thirty kids and shrank to about twelve.

qa.q: What does Kusum reading the sheet aloud and going home on time suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels discouraged and has given up offering her own ideas, perhaps sensing they would not count under the typed sheets.

qa.q: What choice did Simran make at the monthly meeting, and why might it work?
qa.a: She showed Irfan the sign-in book and asked for each person to plan one Saturday; tying the request to attendance, not to his style, made him willing to try.

qa.q: How might Irfan see his typed sheets after turning back through the register?
qa.a: Irfan may start to wonder whether the sheets cost the library its crowds; 'One Saturday' suggests cautious openness.

grounding: Shows a staff member watching a leader decide every detail, colleagues losing initiative and attendance falling, and feedback built on results.

passage:
Dear Pradeep,
Thank you for asking for feedback in Monday's meeting. I've thought about it and want to be useful rather than vague. Over the last quarter, every design decision, down to button colours, has gone through you. The result I'm seeing: our release slipped twice while items waited for sign-off, and the team has stopped proposing solutions; in reviews, people now say "whatever you prefer". I don't think that's what you want. One idea: could small changes go ahead without review, with you looking at a weekly summary? I'd be glad to trial it on my module first.
Best,
Dolma

qa.q: How many times did the release slip?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What is Dolma worried about in the team?
qa.a: Dolma is worried that the team feels helpless and has stopped proposing solutions.

qa.q: Why is Dolma's feedback likely to be heard?
qa.a: It focuses on results like slipped releases and offers a trial, instead of criticising Pradeep's personality.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel reading the email?
qa.a: Pradeep may feel a little stung, but respected, since the feedback is specific and offers a practical way forward.

grounding: Shows a team member observing a manager who decides everything and framing feedback around results.

passage: You asked what it's like on Dilnaz's team. Honestly? She's brilliant, and she decides everything. Font sizes. Who sits in which meeting. Whether a comma goes here. I'm Lalit, and I've been there a year. At first we argued. Now nobody does. Last week a client emailed a simple question, and four of us waited two days for Dilnaz to answer it, because that's what we've learned. The project's late. People are bored. I once told her she was "a control freak". That went badly. So at my review I tried different words: "The Singh project was delayed nine days waiting for approvals. If I can sign off small changes, we'd save time." She actually wrote it down.

qa.q: How many days was the Singh project delayed?
qa.a: Nine days.

qa.q: How does Lalit feel about working on Dilnaz's team?
qa.a: Lalit feels frustrated and bored, noticing the team has learned to wait instead of acting.

qa.q: What went wrong the first time, and what worked better?
qa.a: Calling Dilnaz a control freak attacked her personality; pointing to the nine-day delay focused on results and was heard.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel hearing the delay framed in days?
qa.a: Dilnaz probably feels less attacked and more able to consider the change, since it's about results.

grounding: Illustrates a team member observing a controlling manager and learning that result-based feedback is heard better.

passage: I'm Noor, and I sit two desks from Kamal-sir, our branch manager, so I see most of it. He reads every loan file himself, even the small ones the officers are trained to clear. He rewrites every customer letter. Last month the queue at our counter stretched out of the door because six files were waiting on his desk. The new officers have stopped even trying to decide; they just stack things in his tray. I don't know why he needs it this way. Maybe he got burned once. At the staff meeting I said, "Our average approval time went from three days to eight since March. Could officers clear files under a set amount?" He frowned, but asked me to send him the numbers.

qa.q: How many files were waiting on Kamal-sir's desk?
qa.a: Six files.

qa.q: What is Noor thinking about Kamal-sir's habits?
qa.a: Noor is concerned and curious, unsure why he needs control and guessing he may have been burned once.

qa.q: Why did Noor's comment in the meeting work?
qa.a: It used a clear result, the jump from three days to eight, and offered a specific change instead of blaming him.

qa.q: What is it like for the new officers under Kamal-sir?
qa.a: They seem to feel helpless and have stopped deciding, just stacking files in his tray.

grounding: Shows a colleague watching a manager decide everything, seeing staff grow helpless, and giving results-based feedback.

passage:
Monday: Zainab watched Tushar, their new manager, rewrite the font on every slide in the client deck at 9 p.m. He approved even the order of coffee. By noon, nobody on the team made a decision without asking him.
Two weeks later: The launch slipped by four days. Zainab noticed Priyank, usually full of ideas, simply waiting. "Why bother? He'll change it anyway." She felt a heavy frustration in her chest.
A month later: In their one-to-one, Zainab chose her words carefully. She didn't say "You're controlling." She said, "When every decision comes to you, we wait, and we lost four days on the launch. Could we each own one area, with a check-in on Fridays?"
Tushar frowned, then pulled up the calendar. "Show me what you'd own first."

qa.q: By how many days did the launch slip?
qa.a: Four days.

qa.q: How did Zainab feel when she saw Priyank simply waiting?
qa.a: She felt a heavy frustration, seeing a usually creative teammate give up because Tushar would change everything anyway.

qa.q: Why was Zainab's feedback likely to be heard?
qa.a: She talked about results, the waiting and the lost four days, instead of calling Tushar controlling, and offered a clear plan with Friday check-ins.

qa.q: How might Tushar see the feedback from his side?
qa.a: Tushar might feel uneasy letting go at first, but because it was about results rather than his personality, he was willing to look at ownership areas.

grounding: Shows a team member observing a manager who decides everything, seeing productivity fall and colleagues give up, and giving results-based feedback.
